strengths: The paper tackles an important computer-vision problem: monocular 3D hand reconstruction under severe self- and object-occlusion, where contextual information can genuinely help resolve ambiguity.

Conditioning a generative hand-pose prior on affordance descriptions is intuitive and potentially useful. Combining object attributes, interaction intent, and grasp taxonomy provides richer context than a single action label.
The refinement strategy preserves visible joints while applying the learned prior to uncertain regions, and the proposed self-/object-occlusion criteria are practically motivated.

On the reported high-occlusion subset, the method reduces PA-MPJPE from 21.3 mm for HaMeR to 16.4 mm, a substantial improvement. The qualitative examples also suggest better reconstruction of some occluded fingers.
The presentation is concise, the overall pipeline is easy to follow, and the figures communicate the main idea effectively.
weaknesses: Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the experimental evidence is far too limited to establish the method convincingly. The sole quantitative study uses only 300 instances from a dataset containing 1.5M images, reports no uncertainty or repeated runs, and provides no justification that this very small evaluation sample is representative.

The practical pipeline depends on ground-truth grasp-taxonomy annotations from HOGraspNet because the VLM reportedly cannot infer them reliably. This conflicts with the framing that affordance descriptions are generated from images and leaves the proposed test-time system dependent on unavailable privileged information. It also makes the gain difficult to attribute to VLM-based reasoning rather than ground-truth label conditioning.

The key claim that rich affordance text is responsible for the improvement is not supported by ablations. There are no comparisons among ground-truth taxonomy alone, VLM attributes alone, raw versus summarized captions, individual affordance fields, shuffled or incorrect text, or one-step versus two-step caption generation. Caption correctness is not evaluated either.

The overall gain over HaMeR is only 0.23 mm in PA-MPJPE (8.51 to 8.28), with effectively no gain in the low-occlusion regime (7.69 to 7.67). Although the high-occlusion result is promising, the paper does not report the number of examples in each bin or statistical significance, so the robustness of that result cannot be assessed.

Baseline coverage is inadequate. The only generative comparison is a modified InterHandGen with its original conditioning removed, which is not clearly a competitive method for this task. The paper lacks comparisons with other contextual, optimization-based, hand-object, or diffusion-guided reconstruction approaches cited in the manuscript.

The method is substantially underspecified for reproducibility: the diffusion objective and sampling equations, architecture dimensions, training schedule, optimizer, data preparation, CLIP representation, prompt templates, 2D fitting loss and weighting, and handling of MANO shape, root pose, and camera parameters are omitted. It is also unclear how fixing selected joints is reconciled with coupled MANO pose parameters.

Important protocol details are ambiguous, including whether hand/object boxes are ground truth or detected, how SAM2 is prompted, whether the VLM and segmentation stages use privileged annotations, how occlusion bins are determined, and whether the 300 evaluated examples were selected before observing results.

The evidence for functional coherence and controllability consists only of qualitative images, including a single small-versus-large mug comparison. There are no contact, penetration, grasp consistency, physical plausibility, diversity, or text-pose alignment metrics.

The claim that the framework “jointly learns affordance descriptions and hand poses” appears inaccurate: descriptions are produced by frozen external VLM/LLM components, while the diffusion model learns pose denoising conditioned on CLIP features. The originality is therefore mainly in combining established components, which raises the evidentiary burden for demonstrating that each component is necessary.

Evaluation uses only one dataset and one initial estimator, with no cross-dataset or cross-estimator study. Generalization beyond HOGraspNet's taxonomy and annotation regime is consequently unestablished. Overall, the idea has merit, but the privileged conditioning, missing ablations, weak baseline coverage, and incomplete specification prevent a convincing acceptance case.

strengths: The paper targets an important and difficult computer-vision problem: recovering heavily occluded hands during hand-object interaction. Using affordance information to constrain ambiguous poses is intuitive and potentially useful.
The proposed combination of a text-conditioned diffusion prior with selective refinement of occluded joints is technically plausible, and preserving visible joints is a sensible design choice.

The subject-disjoint S1 evaluation and breakdown by occlusion severity are appropriate. The reported improvement in the high-occlusion subset is substantial, reducing PA-MPJPE from 21.3 mm for HaMeR to 16.4 mm.

The manuscript is concise and generally readable, with figures that communicate the pipeline clearly. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/876ab46b3a3948559b0aa2a82cf81c9b/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central experimental setup appears to use ground-truth grasp-taxonomy annotations when constructing the affordance descriptions, because the VLM cannot predict them reliably. This is privileged test-time information and conflicts with the abstract and figures, which imply that descriptions are inferred from images by a VLM. Consequently, the results do not establish a deployable image-to-pose method, and the gain may largely reflect label leakage.

The empirical evidence is far too limited for the claims. Evaluation uses only 300 instances from one dataset, with no subset counts, repeated sampling, uncertainty estimates, or statistical analysis. The overall improvement over HaMeR is only 0.23 mm in PA-MPJPE, while the low-occlusion gain is 0.02 mm; describing the method as consistently or substantially improving reconstruction is therefore overstated outside the high-occlusion subset.

The comparison does not isolate the proposed contribution. There is only HaMeR and one modified unconditional InterHandGen baseline. Missing controls include predicted versus ground-truth descriptions, taxonomy-only conditioning, categorical affordance conditioning, simple CLIP/image or object conditioning, random or mismatched text, and ablations of occlusion masking and the adaptive noise schedule.

The method is substantially underspecified. The paper omits the diffusion training objective and parameterization, refinement equations, 2D-fitting loss, optimization procedure, architecture dimensions, training hyperparameters, prompt templates, caption post-processing, and sampling details. These omissions make technical verification and reproduction difficult.

The claimed novelty is modest: the architecture is described as InterHandGen with its counter-hand condition replaced by CLIP text, while refinement follows prior work. The manuscript also claims to jointly learn affordance descriptions and hand poses, but the descriptions are produced separately by frozen VLM/LLM components rather than learned jointly.

The assertions of functional coherence and physical plausibility are unsupported by object-aware evaluation. No contact, penetration, grasp consistency, or object-relative pose metric is reported, even though these properties are central to the stated contribution. PA-MPJPE alone also removes global alignment errors and cannot establish a physically valid grasp.

Caption quality and robustness are not evaluated. The pipeline assumes hand-object bounding boxes, SAM2 masks, and reliable VLM-derived object attributes, yet provides no annotation-source details, accuracy measurements, failure analysis, or sensitivity experiments for these inputs.

The controllability evidence consists of a single small-versus-large qualitative pair. Likewise, the refinement visualization contains only four selected examples and lacks comparisons with the unconditional diffusion baseline. This is insufficient to support broad claims of controllable, interpretable generation.

Given the privileged taxonomy input, weak baseline coverage, very small evaluation sample, and lack of ablations, the current evidence does not convincingly demonstrate that affordance-aware textual conditioning itself causes the reported improvement. These are consequential shortcomings rather than minor presentation issues.

strengths: The paper presents a well-motivated Algorithms/General contribution: using affordance-aware language as a generative prior is an intuitive way to address hand-pose ambiguity under object and self-occlusion.
The proposed conditioning is richer than action or object-category labels, combining object properties, interaction type, intention, and a detailed grasp taxonomy.
The largest reported benefit occurs in the intended difficult regime: high-occlusion PA-MPJPE improves from 21.3 mm for HaMeR to 16.4 mm, compared with 19.0 mm for the text-free diffusion baseline.

Selective refinement of occluded joints while preserving visible joints is sensible, and the combination of self-occlusion reasoning and object-mask overlap provides a practical mechanism for identifying uncertain joints.

The manuscript is concise and visually clear. Its qualitative examples suggest reduced errors in occluded fingers, while the controlled generation example provides preliminary evidence that the learned prior responds to object-size language.
weaknesses: The evaluation uses ground-truth grasp-taxonomy annotations because the VLM cannot reliably predict them. This is a major oracle assumption at test time and gives the proposed method privileged pose-relevant information unavailable to HaMeR or a realistic end-to-end system. Accuracy with predicted taxonomy, taxonomy-free descriptions, and deliberately corrupted labels is essential to establish practical benefit.

The quantitative evaluation contains only 300 instances despite HOGraspNet having 1.5M images. Counts for each occlusion subset, repeated sampling, error bars, and statistical tests are absent. Consequently, the small overall improvement over HaMeR—8.51 to 8.28 mm—and the 0.02 mm low-occlusion gain are not convincingly significant.

The experimental comparison is narrow: the only refinement baseline is a simplified, unconditional adaptation of InterHandGen. There are no comparisons to alternative conditional priors or optimization/refinement approaches, and no ablations separating the effects of text, grasp taxonomy, other affordance fields, occlusion-aware joint selection, noise scheduling, or 2D fitting.

Several potentially privileged inputs are insufficiently specified. The VLM receives hand and object bounding boxes, but the paper does not state whether these are ground truth or detected at evaluation. The occlusion procedure also depends on SAM2 masks and projected initial joints, yet neither mask/detection errors nor oracle-versus-predicted inputs are analyzed.

The claim of functionally coherent reconstruction is supported mainly by visual examples. There are no contact, penetration, grasp-class consistency, physical-plausibility, or human-evaluation metrics, and the controllability evidence consists of only one small-versus-large mug example.

Technical and reproducibility details are inadequate: training objectives and data construction, diffusion schedule and sampling equations, classifier-free guidance if any, 2D fitting loss, treatment of MANO global pose and shape, optimizer and training duration, prompts, caption quality, and inference cost are omitted. The paper also says the framework “jointly learns” descriptions and poses, although the descriptions appear to be produced by frozen external models.

Originality is promising but incremental at the algorithmic level: the architecture is adapted from InterHandGen, the refinement strategy follows prior work, and CLIP text conditioning is established. Given the oracle taxonomy and limited empirical validation, the current evidence slightly favors rejection despite the strong concept and encouraging high-occlusion result.
